we find evidence of a possible correlation between Be depletion and planet formation, with a possible shift of this effect toward cooler temperatures (T eff < 5000 K) than for Li.

In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the processes that affect the chemical composition of the stellar surface and, in this way, we hope to contribute to the knowledge of the formation and evolution of planetary systems.
the study of the depletion of Be in stars with planetary companions and the possible differences between stars with and without planetary companions.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the depletion of Be in solar-type stars depends on stellar mass, metallicity, and the presence of a planetary system.

Be depletion in stars with planetary companions is enhanced with respect to stars with similar parameters without detected planets, and that this effect may be more evident for stars with lower effective temperatures.
Be depletion in cool stars is not affected by the presence of a planetary companion, but it may happen in the case of the only cool star with planets in our sample.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the depletion of Li in stars with planets is a general phenomenon, while the depletion of Be seems to be a more specific effect.
the Be depletion is not a function of stellar metallicity, but rather a function of stellar temperature, and that the Be depletion may also be affected by the presence of planetary systems.
Be is depleted in the convective envelopes of cool stars with planets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Be abundance of cool stars with planetary companions is enhanced with respect to stars of the same effective temperature but without planets.
Be may also be affected, and that it is important to study its abundance for a larger sample of cool stars with and without exoplanets.
Be depletion may be a good tracer of the presence of planets around cool stars, as it is in the Sun.
